final_message:
All three versions are done and verified. Summary:

**Algorithm (all three)**
Parse the rates line, then stream transactions: skip `void` / tags containing `"test"`, convert amount to hundredths, `usd = hundredths * rate // 1_000_000` (exact integer math, sign applied after division), aggregate count/net globally, per channel, and per account; emit channels sorted by name and the top 10 accounts by (net desc, id asc). The key correctness trap is that nested decoy objects contain fake `account`/`type`/`tags`/`channel` fields, so every parser is depth-aware and only reads top-level fields plus `meta.channel`, with full JSON string unescaping (`\uXXXX`, surrogate pairs) for compared/stored strings.

**Speed choices per version**
- [rust/src/main.rs](D:\projects\nb-work\39-rust-vs-python\sessions\wonder\ledger\rust\src\main.rs): hand-rolled zero-copy byte scanner over the whole file in memory — no JSON DOM, ignored values skipped structurally, string contents kept as slices into the input (decoded only when escapes are present), FxHash maps, linear scan for the few channels, single buffered output write. Rates line (tiny) uses `serde_json`. Release profile: LTO + `codegen-units=1` + `panic="abort"` in [rust/Cargo.toml](D:\projects\nb-work\39-rust-vs-python\sessions\wonder\ledger\rust\Cargo.toml).
- [plain.py](D:\projects\nb-work\39-rust-vs-python\sessions\wonder\ledger\plain.py): idiomatic stdlib — one `read().decode().split("\n")`, C `json.loads` per line (measured faster than any Python-level scanner; a regex tokenizer was 4× slower than `json`), manual hundredths parsing avoiding floats, dict aggregation in the same loop.
- [fast.py](D:\projects\nb-work\39-rust-vs-python\sessions\wonder\ledger\fast.py): same C JSON core via a bound `JSONDecoder.decode`, but the loop only appends to column lists (with channel/account interned to integer ids); NumPy then does the conversion `(h * r // 1_000_000) * s` and exact int64 group sums via argsort+cumsum segment sums (`np.add.at` and string `np.unique` were measured slower and dropped). Output is written via `sys.stdout.buffer` in both Python versions — text-mode stdout on Windows would emit CRLF, while expected output is LF-only.

**Verification** — byte-exact against expected output (not just line-equal):
- Samples `s1`, `s2`, `s3`: Rust, plain, and fast all pass.
- Extra generated cases (3005-line adversarial file with escaped field values like `"cred\u0069t"`, escaped `"te\u0073t"` skip tags, decoys before real fields, surrogate pairs, tie sums, <10 accounts; plus rates-only file, all-skipped file, and missing-final-newline file): all three agree byte-exactly with an independent reference.

Indicative timing on a 250k-line / 95 MB input (noisy shared machine, best of interleaved runs): Rust ~0.7s, plain ~3.4s, fast ~3.5–4.0s — in-process A/B shows fast's loop beats plain's, but NumPy import + stage costs roughly cancel that at this size; both Pythons are bounded by the ~10 µs/line C JSON parse.

request.prompt:
You are writing three versions of the same program, one in Rust and two in Python, for a comparison of how
fast and how memory-hungry each version is.

The task is described in SPEC.md in this folder. The folder samples/ holds example inputs (`*.in`), each with
the exact expected output (`*.out`).

Write these three files:

1. `rust/src/main.rs`: Rust, compiled with rustc 1.99 (edition 2024). The Cargo project in `rust/` is set
   up. The only crates you may use are serde (with derive), serde_json, regex and rayon. They are already
   listed in `rust/Cargo.toml` and vendored, so build offline with `cargo build --release --offline` inside
   `rust/`. Do not add other dependencies. You may change the `[profile.release]` settings in
   `rust/Cargo.toml`.
2. `plain.py`: Python 3.13, standard library only.
3. `fast.py`: Python 3.13, standard library plus NumPy 2.2.

Each program is run with the path of one input file as its argument (SPEC.md says if a task takes more
arguments). It reads that file and writes the answer to standard output exactly as SPEC.md describes. The
Python versions are run as `C:\Python313\python.exe plain.py INPUT_PATH` and
`C:\Python313\python.exe fast.py INPUT_PATH`, and the Rust version as the release binary
`rust/target/release/solution.exe INPUT_PATH`.

Your goals, in order:

1. Every version must print the correct output for any valid input as SPEC.md defines it, not only for the
   samples.
2. Make each version as fast as you can. Write each one the way a skilled developer in that language would
   write fast code, using that language's own strengths.

Use a single thread and a single process unless SPEC.md says otherwise. Do not precompute or embed answers,
start other programs, or read any file other than the input.

The programs will be run on Windows 11 on a 16-core laptop, on larger inputs of the same kind; SPEC.md gives
the benchmark size. Test all three versions against every sample before you finish. Work only inside this
folder, and take at most about 45 minutes. Other programs run on this machine at the same time:
never stop a process you did not start yourself, so do not kill processes by name (for example
`taskkill /IM python.exe` or `Stop-Process -Name python`); stop only your own processes, by process ID.

When you are done, reply with a short summary: the algorithm, the main choices you made for speed in each
version, and which samples each version passes.
